title: Can, Could, May
subtitle: Talk about ability, permission, and polite requests.
objectives: Use can for present ability and informal permission
Use could for past ability and polite requests
Use may for formal permission and possibility

content.intro: These three small words let you talk about what people are able to do, what they're allowed to do, and how to ask for things politely.

rules.heading: a) Can
rules.body:
• Present ability: She can speak three languages.
  • Informal permission: Can I open the window?

rules.heading: b) Could
rules.body:
• Past ability: They could play the guitar when they were younger.
  • Polite requests: Could you help me with my homework?

rules.heading: c) May
rules.body:
• Formal permission: May I go to the bathroom?
  • Possibility: It may rain later.

examples: Can you help me with my homework?
She can speak three languages fluently.
Could I borrow your pen, please?
They could play the guitar when they were younger.
May I go to the bathroom?
It may rain later this afternoon.

commonMistakes.wrong: She can to speak three languages.
commonMistakes.why: Modal verbs (can, could, may) are never followed by "to" — use the bare infinitive.
Modal verbs never add -s, even for he/she/it.
After "could," use the base form of the verb, not the past form.
After "can," use the base form of the verb, not the -ing form.

exercises.title: Fill in the Blanks
exercises.instructions: Complete each sentence with can, could, or may.

items.prompt: ___ you help me with my homework?
items.explanation: Both work here as a request, "could" being more polite/formal.

items.prompt: They ___ play the guitar when they were younger.
___ I go to the bathroom? (formal, asking the teacher)
items.explanation: "May" is the more formal option; "can" is also commonly accepted.

items.prompt: It ___ rain later — the sky looks dark.
___ you swim when you were five?

items.incorrect: She can to swim very well.
items.explanation: Never use "to" after a modal verb.

summary: Modal verbs are always followed by the bare infinitive — never "to," never -s, never -ing.
